title: Teaching notes: Day 1
text:
A slightly deeper tornado orientation
The three-minute introduction covers details that influence the analysis:

One row is one whole tornado track. Extra state/county continuation records and one exact duplicate were removed in preparation. A track can cross state lines. Starting state does not list all states affected.
Types carry meaning. The identifier is a label, EF is ordered, state is nominal, and length and width are quantities with different units. Do not infer measurement meaning from a column’s storage dtype alone.
Clock time is CST for every record. Comparing CST hours does not automatically compare local daylight or nighttime.
Missing ratings stay missing. EF0 is valid. There are 111 unknown ratings, leaving 4,595 records with an observed rating. Students should decide whether their question requires those values before filtering.

EF categories reflect damage surveys and estimated winds. They are not direct wind measurements, and a larger category number is not a ratio of wind speeds. Source: https://www.weather.gov/oun/efscale.
The starter shows a few rows, column information and missingness, but no substantive tornado analysis. This gives students a foundation without steering their question choice.

title: Teaching notes: Day 1
text:
The investigation
During brainstorming, reward distinct questions that students can connect to available fields. Offer general prompts only if needed: distribution, comparison, relationship, time or space, unusual observations, and missingness.
When groups select a question, ask which rows, variables, units, comparison, and any denominator would provide evidence. Words like dangerous or worst need a measurable definition.
At around minute 25 ask what the first visualization leaves unresolved. At around minute 32 ask everyone to prepare their plot and explanation for regrouping.
Circulation prompts:

What do you actually see in this view?
What does that leave unresolved?
How many records support the comparison?
Which observations drive the result?
What other view would help distinguish your explanations?

Use the separate plotting reference for syntax support. Avoid supplying a shared tornado question or a worked tornado result.

title: Teaching notes: Day 1
text:
Sharing and closing
Randomly regroup students, aiming for groups of 3-4 from different original teams. Allow one minute to move, about two minutes per person, and remaining time for follow-up questions. Every student explains their original team’s work independently.
The closing asks for a visualization that changed a question, something the data could not fully answer, or a useful approach learned from someone else. A well-explained inconclusive result is useful.
Bridge to Day 2: we compared Titanic passengers a few variables at a time. Next we will explore similarity across several characteristics together, then investigate how those profiles relate to survival.

EF ratings and missing information
EF0 through EF5 are ordered damage categories associated with estimated winds.
EF0 is valid. An unknown rating is missing, not zero.
This snapshot has 111 unknown ratings. Keep those records until your question requires a decision about them.

The bundled titanic.csv contains 891 passenger records from the seaborn example dataset, a familiar subset associated with the Kaggle Titanic training data. It is a subset of Titanic passengers, not a complete passenger manifest or a random sample of everyone aboard.

sex preserves the source’s recorded categories. survived is 1 for survived and 0 otherwise. fare is the recorded fare in pounds sterling, with possible shared-ticket complications.
The seaborn-data repository describes these files as example datasets and cautions that some are modified from their canonical sources: https://github.com/mwaskom/seaborn-data

title: Data sources and preparation
text:
Tornado group investigation
The old slides contain a Wikipedia table for 2015-2022 but do not include the underlying data file. This package uses a 2015-2018 NOAA Storm Prediction Center snapshot instead. It does not contain city names, narrative summaries, or end times. The change in coverage and schema is explicit throughout these materials.

Primary publisher: NOAA / National Weather Service Storm Prediction Center, Severe Weather Database, https://www.spc.noaa.gov/wcm/#data
Field specification: https://www.spc.noaa.gov/wcm/data/SPC_severe_database_description.pdf
Accessible copy of that specification: https://www.gsa.state.al.us/apps/CAGDV/Metadata/Hazards/SPC_severe_database_description.pdf
Annual NOAA CSV snapshots obtained from the teaching repository https://github.com/gabrielodom/PHC6701_r4ds/tree/main/_data/purrr_example_data
Original files: raw/2015_torn.csv through raw/2018_torn.csv.
The four annual snapshots contain 4,820 rows including state and county continuation segments. Keep sg == 1 to retain whole tracks, then remove one exact duplicate. This produces 4,706 records.
NOAA/SPC is the data publisher. The GitHub repository is the retrieval mirror, not a separate observing system. Treat this as a historical snapshot that can differ from later NOAA revisions.
Federal NOAA data are public domain. Credit NOAA/SPC when reusing the data. General NOAA guidance: https://www.noaa.gov/information-technology/open-data-dissemination

title: Data sources and preparation
text:
Preparation choices
Run python scripts/prepare_data.py from the repository root to recreate the teaching CSVs from the bundled raw snapshots. No network access is needed.

Retain whole-track rows (sg == 1). Extra state and continuing county segments would otherwise count some tornadoes more than once.
Remove the one exact duplicate. Validate the resulting year-event identifier.
Rename fields and add tornado_id and start_hour_cst.
Recode EF rating -9 as missing. Preserve 0 as the valid EF0 category.
Recode zero latitude or longitude as missing. Preserve recorded zero path measurements rather than assigning an undocumented meaning to them.
Omit monetary loss fields because the source’s units and coding change across years.
Omit county codes and narrative fields absent from this snapshot.

All retained source records use timezone code 3, which the SPC specification defines as Central Standard Time. The hour is therefore CST for every record, not local clock time at each tornado location. No daylight saving adjustment is applied.
start_state names the state attached to the whole-track record, associated with the tornado’s start. A tornado can affect more than one state. Counts by this column are counts assigned to the starting state, not counts of all tornadoes affecting each state.
The preparation manifest records row counts and SHA-256 hashes. The snapshot has 111 unknown EF ratings, retained as missing. For analyses requiring EF, report the number of excluded records. Geographic comparisons of raw counts do not account for area, population, or reporting differences. These four years support descriptive investigation, not a long-term climate trend claim.
